posts.post_text: We banned ChatGPT in our analytics department last month. Not because AI is bad — because nobody could explain where the numbers came from. When a regulator asks 'how did you arrive at this figure?' and the answer is 'GPT said so', you've got a compliance problem. The AI trust gap is real and growing.
posts.angle: High-scoring post with three ICP prospects engaging in a compliance-heavy context — validate the explainability problem as the real blocker, not AI itself
posts.draft_comment: The ban wasn't really about ChatGPT. It was about numbers showing up in a room with no audit trail behind them. Regulators don't want to hear 'the model said so' — they want a chain of logic they can walk back step by step. How many analytics teams do you think are still one awkward question away from the same outcome?

posts.post_text: We spent 18 months building a Power BI dashboard that our finance team refuses to use. They still export everything to Excel and email it around. The building part was easy. Getting people to actually trust the numbers enough to quote them in a board meeting? That's the real challenge nobody talks about. Anyone else hit this wall?
posts.angle: ICP prospect COO at 140-person firm hitting the trust wall with Power BI — validate the pain sharply, add the insight that adoption is a trust problem not a training problem
posts.draft_comment: The dashboard was never the hard part. It's that finance teams have been burned before — a number looked wrong once, someone questioned a formula in a meeting, and now the spreadsheet feels safer because at least they built it themselves. You can't train your way out of that. The question is whether the tool earns trust or just asks for it.

posts.post_text: Unpopular opinion: most operational dashboards are vanity projects. We had 47 KPIs on our ops dashboard. Nobody looked at it. Cut it to 5 metrics that actually drive decisions. Usage went from 10% to 85%. The problem with BI isn't the tools — it's that we measure everything and understand nothing.
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Director of Operations at Summit Group) engaging with a post about dashboard bloat — validate the 47-to-5 insight, add the 'measurement vs understanding' layer, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: 47 KPIs is basically a defence mechanism — if everything matters, nobody has to own anything. The 10% to 85% usage jump tells you everything about what happens when people actually trust what they're looking at. The hard question most ops teams never ask is: are we measuring this because it drives a decision, or because someone once asked for it in a meeting?

posts.post_text: Hot take: self-service BI is a myth. We gave everyone Power BI licenses and what happened? 200 reports, zero consistency, three different definitions of 'revenue'. The promise of democratising data is great until you realise nobody agrees on what the data means. Build vs buy isn't the question — it's 'who owns the truth?'
posts.angle: High-scoring post with Innovation Director ICP engaging — validate the 'who owns the truth' framing and reframe the real failure as a governance problem, not a tooling problem
posts.draft_comment: The 200 reports problem isn't a Power BI problem, it's what happens when you hand out tools before anyone's agreed what the numbers mean. Most companies skip that conversation entirely because it's harder than buying licenses. The tech was never the bottleneck — getting finance, ops, and marketing to agree on one definition of revenue is almost a political problem. Wonder if anyone's actually solved that without someone quite senior owning it full-time?

posts.post_text: AI hallucinations in analytics are a security issue, not just an accuracy issue. If your AI tool generates a financial report with hallucinated numbers and someone makes a decision based on it, that's not a bug — it's a material risk. We need to start treating AI outputs with the same scrutiny as we treat user inputs.
posts.angle: CISO at a healthcare org reframing AI hallucinations as a security risk — validate the framing with a sharper operational angle, with a CEO at a 90-person data company watching
posts.draft_comment: The framing here is right and I think it's actually undersold. A hallucinated number in a dashboard doesn't announce itself — it looks exactly like a real number, sits in the same report, gets the same confidence. We've spent years building controls around who can access data. Barely anyone is asking who's responsible when the data the AI surfaces was never real to begin with.

posts.post_text: Had a fascinating conversation with a client yesterday. They spent £200k on a BI platform and the only person who can use it is the one who built it. Self-service my arse. The gap between what vendors promise and what actually happens in a 50-person company is enormous. When will the industry admit that most BI tools are built for data teams, not business teams?
posts.angle: ICP prospect Helen Cross (COO at Sterling Consulting) engaging with a post about BI tools failing non-technical users — validate the £200k waste pattern, add the real reason it happens, leave her thinking
posts.draft_comment: That £200k story is painfully common. The dirty secret is most BI tools are optimised for the person building dashboards, not the person who needs to make a decision at 8am before a client call. So the builder becomes the bottleneck, and suddenly you've bought yourself a very expensive dependency. What does success even look like when the CFO still screenshots the dashboard and pastes it into a slide?

posts.post_text: Just had our quarterly review and the CFO asked why the numbers in our BI dashboard don't match the numbers in the ERP. Turns out three different teams were applying different filters to the same dataset. AI won't fix this. Culture will. But nobody wants to hear that.
posts.angle: Commercial Director at a likely mid-market industrial company has surfaced the single biggest trust-killer in BI — validate that it's a people/process problem, not a data problem, and add the sharper observation that most tools make this worse by hiding the filters entirely
posts.draft_comment: Three teams, one dataset, three different answers — that's not a data quality problem, that's a visibility problem. Most dashboards show you the number but bury how it was calculated, so nobody even knows there's a filter to disagree about. Culture helps, but only once people can actually see what assumptions went into the figure. Did your CFO ever trust the dashboard before this, or was this the moment it crystallised?

posts.post_text: Rolled out Copilot to 500 users last quarter. Usage after 90 days? 12%. The problem isn't the tool — it's that nobody knows what to ask it. We're essentially paying for a very expensive autocomplete. Shadow AI is the real story here — people are using ChatGPT on their phones because Copilot is too locked down.
posts.angle: IT Director surfacing the real adoption failure mode (nobody knows what to ask) — validate the shadow AI insight and add the deeper 'wrong mental model' layer without pitching
posts.draft_comment: The 12% number is almost always a 'what do I even ask' problem, not a features problem. People open Copilot, stare at a blank prompt, and close it — then go back to the spreadsheet they already understand. Shadow AI makes total sense in that context, it's lower stakes to experiment on your phone. The real question is whether the org ever closes the gap between having data access and knowing what questions are worth asking.
